approachQuestion.prompt:
Container Membership. A non-empty rooted binary tree has IDs 0 through n-1. A supplied nodes array maps each ID directly to its node. Given q pairs (u,v), return for each whether u is an ancestor of v, allowing u=v. Answer many queries on the same immutable hierarchy.

In examples, x(left,right) denotes a node labelled x, and - denotes an absent child. Example 1: Input: 0(1(3(-,-),-),2(-,-)), queries=[(1,3),(3,1),(2,2),(1,2)]. Output: [true,false,true,false]. Example 2: Input: 0(-,-), queries=[(0,0)]. Output: [true].

Constraints: 1 <= n <= 200000; 1 <= q <= 200000; every query ID is valid. The tree has child pointers only, no parent pointers, cycles or shared nodes; shape is unrestricted. The nodes array, query array and output Boolean array are supplied. Preprocessing for this query batch is allowed; do not change the tree.

options.text: Make one depth-first traversal with entry and exit events. Store an entry number and completed-subtree boundary for each ID. Answer a query by testing whether v’s entry lies inside u’s interval.
options.feedback: A depth-first traversal finishes every descendant before leaving its subtree. Those entries form one contiguous interval, including the node itself.

options.text: For each query separately traverse the subtree rooted at nodes[u] and look for v, including u itself.
options.feedback: This answers every query correctly and uses the hierarchy, but repeats work across the batch. Precomputed subtree intervals reuse one traversal for all queries.

options.text: Record only entry numbers. Return true whenever entry[u] <= entry[v].
options.feedback: In Example 1 a left-first traversal enters 1 before 2, but 1 is not an ancestor of 2. A subtree end boundary is also needed.

options.text: Return true whenever u<=v, because IDs encode the hierarchy order.
options.feedback: No such ID ordering is promised. In Example 1, 1<=2 but 1 does not contain 2.

feedback.reason: Entry and completion intervals answer repeated ancestor queries without rescanning paths.
details: Use explicit depth-first frames with enter and exit phases. At entry set tin[id] to a counter and increment it. At exit set end[id] to the current counter. Store these in arrays indexed by ID. For each query return tin[u] <= tin[v] and tin[v] < end[u]. Use no hashing or copied paths.

Depth-first entry indices put every subtree in one contiguous half-open interval. u contains v exactly when tin[v] lies in u's interval, including u itself. Exit boundaries exclude nodes visited after the subtree finishes.

“Make one depth-first traversal with entry and exit events. Store an entry number and completed-subtree boundary for each ID. Answer a query by testing whether v’s entry lies inside u’s interval.”: A depth-first traversal finishes every descendant before leaving its subtree. Those entries form one contiguous interval, including the node itself.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the revealed interval method let n be the node count, h the height and q the query count. Include the entire preprocessing and all query answers. What is the tight worst-case pair? Count the two length-n arrays and traversal frames; exclude the supplied tree, nodes array, query array and final Boolean output array. Output slots are preallocated.
constraints: All legal shapes are allowed; do not assume balance. Heights count nodes, not edges.

Pointer access, comparisons, arithmetic on the stated integer ranges, and allocation/release of a fixed-size frame take constant time. No hashing is used. Count all live explicit frames; the method does not use language recursion or copy paths/subtrees unless explicitly stated.

options.text: O(n log n + q) time, O(n) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Prepare two n-entry time arrays once and answer q interval tests.
details: There are O(n) traversal events and O(q) constant-time comparisons. Two length-n arrays plus O(h) frames use O(n) space because h<=n.
Entries between tin[u] inclusive and end[u] exclusive are exactly the nodes visited before u’s depth-first exit, hence exactly its subtree. This includes u and no later sibling subtree.
“O(nq) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: That time corresponds to repeated subtree searches. Preprocessing visits each node once and each interval query is constant-time.
“O(n+q) time, O(h) auxiliary space”: The explicit frames are not the only storage: both timestamp arrays remain live for the queries.
“O(n+q) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: There are O(n) traversal events and O(q) constant-time comparisons. Two length-n arrays plus O(h) frames use O(n) space because h<=n.
“O(n log n + q) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: IDs index arrays directly; no sorting, binary searches, or ordered-map operations are performed.
